summary: We developed Lunar Landing Site Navigator, an interactive Python and Streamlit decision-support tool with 3D visualizations for evaluating candidate landing sites at the Moon's South Pole. Using NASA LRO LOLA elevation data and topocentric ephemeris calculations, our platform models local horizon profiles, solar illumination, shadow casting, photovoltaic power output, and Direct-to-Earth (DTE) line-of-sight communication windows across lunar libration cycles. It also integrates a Monte Carlo landing ellipse simulation to quantify touchdown dispersion and compute probabilistic site viability scores. Because the Moon's ~1.54° axial tilt produces permanent shadows in crater floors alongside grazing sunlight and low-horizon Earth geometry, selecting safe zones is critical. Our application enables mission planners to rapidly assess terrain hazards, energy availability, and communication reliability to reduce risk for future lunar missions.
details:
What It Does & How It Works

Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive decision-support platform designed to evaluate and compare candidate landing sites at the Moon's South Pole. Built with a modular Python architecture, the system integrates four core analytical engines into a unified 3D dashboard:

1. Topocentric Ephemeris Engine: Computes high-precision Solar and Earth azimuth and elevation angles over custom mission windows using astronomical ephemeris models.

2. Terrain & Horizon Profiling: Processes lunar elevation data to extract 360° local horizon obstruction profiles around candidate coordinates.

3. Illumination, Shadow & Power Modeling: Simulates dynamic solar illumination, shadow casting, photovoltaic power generation, and Direct-to-Earth (DTE) line-of-sight communication windows.

4. Probabilistic Risk Analyzer: Runs Monte Carlo landing ellipse simulations to quantify touchdown dispersion, terrain slope/roughness hazards, and composite site viability scores.

Factors Considered & Creative Approach

Operating near the lunar South Pole presents extreme physical constraints because the Moon's ~1.54° axial tilt causes sunlight to graze the horizon nearly horizontally—creating permanently shadowed crater floors alongside elevated rims with extended illumination—while Earth undergoes slow apparent vertical oscillations (lunar libration) near the horizon. Rather than evaluating lighting, communications, or terrain slope in isolation, our creative approach couples deterministic orbital mechanics and topographic ray-tracing with stochastic Monte Carlo touchdown dispersion in a real-time 3D interactive environment.

Benefits & Intended Impact

Mission planners and researchers can rapidly screen South Pole landing zones, visualize terrain hazards in 3D, and quantify trade-offs between solar energy availability, continuous Earth visibility, and landing safety—helping reduce operational risk and planning time for future robotic and crewed lunar exploration missions.

Tools, Languages, Software & Data Used

- Programming Language: Python

- Frameworks & Visualization: Streamlit, Plotly (3D surface and analytical charts), Pydeck

- Scientific & Geospatial Libraries: Astropy, Skyfield, Rasterio, NumPy, SciPy

- Dataset: NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) – Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) elevation subsets and South Pole candidate site coordinates

- Development & Version Control: Git, GitHub, Linux (Fedora), Neovim

Super Intelligence (SI) Disclosure

Generative AI (Google Gemini) was utilized during development to assist with modular code scaffolding, Streamlit/Plotly visualization debugging, Git workflow troubleshooting, and documentation formatting. All physical equations, astronomical calculations, datasets, and outputs were independently reviewed, tested, and validated by Team Schnauzers.
